layers.name: Product Composition Seam
layers.description: The two product shells (apps/sif and apps/codewall, selected by Vite --mode) and the shared src/app seam they both fan into — mount, routes, sections, the lazy page registry, and the ProductDefinition contract that carries product identity as a plain object rather than build flags.

layers.name: Route Screens
layers.description: Production route-level screens under src/pages — rulesets, policies, rules, agents, API keys, access control, audit log and the rest — each composing design-system primitives with React Query hooks (demo-only screens live in the Demo Mode layer).

layers.name: Composed Components
layers.description: Domain-aware composites and dialogs in src/components — rule and policy editors, API key editors, match-spec builders, provenance panels — that know about SIF concepts and call the API, unlike the product-neutral primitives beneath them.

layers.name: Design System
layers.description: Product-neutral presentation primitives in src/ui plus the src/index.css design tokens; its index.ts barrel is the single most-imported module in the codebase (66 importers) and the layer holds no API or auth knowledge.

layers.name: API Transport & Contract
layers.description: The HTTP transport seam: src/api/client.ts with its 28 endpoint definitions (mostly under the /manage prefix, with /api/health, /api/version, /manage/auth/sso-status and /platform/tenants deliberately outside it), the shared wire types, and the adapters that normalise dates, threat payloads and attention state.

layers.name: Server State & Caching
layers.description: Cache policy sitting above transport — the 49 exported React Query hooks in queries.ts, the shared QueryClient singleton, and the polling and WebSocket hooks that decide staleness, refetch cadence and live updates for every screen.

layers.name: Session & Access Control
layers.description: Cross-cutting authentication and RBAC: session and token refresh, the capabilities hook that 29 modules consult before rendering an action, and the forbidden pub/sub that turns a 403 into a single application-wide response.

layers.name: In-App Docs Viewer
layers.description: The self-contained docs-reading feature (not project documentation): command palette, overlay panel with focus management, markdown rendering, plain-text extraction and the ranked search over a build-generated index — the most internally cohesive module in the tree.

layers.name: Demo Mode
layers.description: The contained, off-by-default demo feature: the sessionStorage gate and demo context, the useDemoQuery shim, the demo payments/network/governance screens and panels, and fixtures reachable only through a dynamic import in loaders.ts — never a live data source.

layers.name: Build & Tooling
layers.description: The two-product build configuration and its guards — Vite config with the dev proxy and per-mode app roots, TypeScript and ESLint settings, the npm manifest, the docs-index generator, and the script that verifies one product build never leaks the other product’s code.

tour.title: Two Products, One Source Tree
tour.description: Start here, because this is the fact that reframes everything else: this package is not one app, it is two. `apps/sif/main.tsx` and `apps/codewall/main.tsx` are separate Vite entry points over the same `src/` tree, each assembling a `ProductDefinition` — product id, presentation strings, extra routes and sections — and handing it to the shared bootstrap. `src/app/types.ts` is that contract, and the important consequence is that product identity travels as a plain object passed downward, not as a build flag read from anywhere. Nothing inside `src/` ever reaches back up into `apps/`, so if you find yourself wanting to import from `apps/` in shared code, you have taken a wrong turn.
tour.languageLesson: `DashboardPages` is a `Record` over a closed `DashboardPageName` union. Adding a page to the registry without listing it in the union — or listing a name with no page behind it — is a compile error, so the two halves of the registry cannot drift apart silently.

tour.title: The Shared Bootstrap and Shell
tour.description: Both entry points from Step 1 converge on `mount.tsx`, the single bootstrap: it stamps the product id onto the document element, loads fonts and global CSS, and renders `App` inside StrictMode and a `BrowserRouter` based at `/dashboard`. `App.tsx` is the shell that owns everything a screen should not: auth token and user state, session expiry and logout, theme persistence, the command palette, the docs panel and the demo switch. `context.tsx` then carries the active `ProductDefinition` down through React context, so a shared component can read product identity without any prop drilling.
tour.languageLesson: Setting `document.documentElement.dataset.product` in `mount.tsx` is what lets one CSS bundle theme both products from a single attribute selector — no per-product stylesheet, no runtime branching in components.

tour.title: Page Registry and Route Tree
tour.description: The route tree is built, not written out by hand. `pages.ts` is a registry of every shared screen as a `React.lazy` component; `sections.ts` returns the four navigation sections — Fleet, Guardrails, Activity, Access; and `routes.tsx` assembles them into a react-router tree, wrapping each section in a capability guard, redirecting legacy paths, and splicing each product's own routes in at the section it names. This is the mechanism that makes Step 1's contract concrete: Codewall adds an Endpoints tab by naming a section, not by editing shared routing code.
tour.languageLesson: `React.lazy` at the registry level means each screen is its own bundle chunk. The demo-only overview pages are registered the same way, so their chunks are simply never fetched while the demo switch is off — see Step 12.

tour.title: Transport: One Client, One Prefix
tour.description: `src/api/` is two distinct layers and conflating them is the most common early mistake — this step is the lower one. `client.ts` is pure transport: an authenticated fetch pipeline (one 401 retry against the refresh token, 403 surfaced as a dismissible RBAC notice) plus roughly eighty thin typed wrappers, one per backend route. Almost every route is a child of a single `MANAGE_BASE = "/manage"` prefix, with four families deliberately outside it — `/api/health`, `/api/version`, `/manage/auth/sso-status` and `/platform/tenants` — which is why `requestUrl` is split out from `request` so the siblings can share the same pipeline. `types.ts` is the TypeScript mirror of the Rust backend's wire contract and has fan-in 38, the second highest in the graph.
tour.languageLesson: `types.ts` is a type-only module with a single value export. Everything else is `interface` or `type`, so it erases completely at build time and costs nothing in the bundle despite being imported nearly everywhere.

tour.title: Cache Policy: Where Caching Lives
tour.description: This is the upper half of `src/api/`, and it is a different job from Step 4. `queries.ts` is the TanStack Query layer — it declares every cache key once, exposes around fifty typed query and mutation hooks, and invalidates precisely, with optimistic rollback on the toggles. Its fan-out of 78 is the largest in the codebase and its fan-in of 29 means nearly every screen consumes it, which is exactly the point: pages hold no server state of their own. `queryClient.ts` sets the 30-second stale time and a deliberate `retry: 1` so a 403 refusal does not fan out into repeated permission notices, and `useStatsSummary.ts` is the shared source for headline counters so two pages showing the same window always show the same number.
tour.languageLesson: Cache keys are declared as const key factories (`rulesetKeys`, `policyKeys`, `ruleLibraryKey`) rather than built from strings at call sites. That is the whole reason invalidation can be targeted rather than blunt — a typo becomes a compile error instead of a stale panel.

tour.title: Session and Capability Gating
tour.description: `session.ts` owns access and refresh token storage and the single-flight refresh that keeps a session alive, emitting token-changed and session-expired events so code outside React's data flow can react. `capabilities.ts` — fan-in 29 — is the UI's RBAC layer: a compile-time capability union, a `can()` predicate, a context provider seeded from `GET /manage/auth/me`, and the `RequireCapability` guard that Step 3's route tree wraps sections in. Read the comment in that file carefully: gating here fails closed and is a usability affordance only, because the server remains the sole enforcement point.
tour.languageLesson: Refresh rotates — the backend revokes the presented session before minting a new pair, so two concurrent refreshes would revoke each other. One shared in-flight promise is what keeps a recoverable expiry recoverable instead of turning it into a surprise logout.

tour.title: The Design System Is Enforced
tour.description: `ui/index.ts` has fan-in 66, the highest in the graph: it is a barrel, and pages import the whole shared vocabulary from it and never from the individual modules, so the design-system surface stays one thing. The rule newcomers break is about colour. `palette.ts` is the only module permitted to hold hex literals — mirrored from the CSS custom properties for chart libraries that cannot resolve `var(--…)` — and `aesthetics.test.ts` fails the build on a hex written anywhere else. Domain facts reach components through `visualState.ts`, a five-value `VisualState` vocabulary with mappings for decision effects, lifecycles, severities and risk scores, so a screen imports a mapping and never a colour. `index.css` is 2061 lines: the token layer plus the whole component vocabulary, with measured contrast ratios recorded in the comments.
tour.languageLesson: Every `visualState` mapper takes `string` rather than its own union, because callers hold server-typed values. An unrecognised input resolves to `neutral`, so an unknown verdict renders as unknown rather than being invented as danger.

tour.title: Composed Domain Components
tour.description: Between the design system of Step 7 and the screens of Step 9 sits `src/components/` — pieces that know about the domain but not about a route. `MatchSpecEditor` is the deepest of them, converting the backend match-spec union to and from a flat editable form state and rendering the controls for every match kind. `RulePicker`, `RuleEditor` and `PolicySet` have the highest fan-in of the group because several screens reuse them; that reuse is why the policy and ruleset screens stay comparatively thin.
tour.languageLesson: `MatchSpecEditor` groups controls with `fieldset`/`legend` rather than nesting several controls inside one `<label>`, so each control keeps its own accessible name. Accessibility conventions like this are load-bearing here, not decorative.

tour.title: A Screen, End to End
tour.description: Now put Steps 4 through 8 together. `Policies.tsx` has the highest fan-out of any screen (17) and is the best worked example: it lists live and archived policies, edits mode, fail mode and threshold bands inline behind a dirty bar, and hosts version history, ruleset attachment and execution-plan editing. Notice what it does not do — it holds no server state, calls no `fetch`, and names no colour; it composes hooks from Step 5, guards from Step 6 and vocabulary from Steps 7 and 8. `Rulesets.tsx` and `Rules.tsx` are the same shape one level down the policy hierarchy.

tour.title: The Home Screen and Live Events
tour.description: `Home.tsx` is the landing screen, and its interesting half is `attention.ts` — a pure derivation layer that turns data the app has already fetched (API keys, rulesets, policies, users) into a ranked queue of `AttentionItem` objects, each carrying a severity, a condition label, the consequence of ignoring it, and a verb plus route to the screen that fixes it. No new endpoint is involved; it is a reading of existing cache. `useWebSocket.ts` is the other live path: it connects with the current access token, buffers events, reconnects on transient drops, and gives up after repeated auth failures rather than looping forever on an expired token.
tour.languageLesson: `useWebSocket` subscribes to the token-changed event from Step 6 via `useSyncExternalStore`, so a background refresh is observed immediately instead of waiting for an unrelated re-render to notice.

tour.title: Audit Trail and Evidence Export
tour.description: `AuditLog.tsx` is the most filter-heavy screen in the app: nine URL-seeded text filters plus a degraded-only toggle over a paginated table, a URL-addressable detail pane, client-side JSON and CSV export of the rows on screen, and `ExportEvidence` for the signed export. It is worth reading as a pattern for URL-as-state, and `dates.ts` is the small shared module that keeps range handling consistent between this screen and the panels beside it.
tour.languageLesson: `TEXT_FILTER_KEYS` is declared `as const` and the `Filters` type is derived from it, so adding a filter key updates the record type, the URL seeding loop and the chip list in a single edit. This is the idiomatic TypeScript alternative to keeping three parallel lists in sync by hand.

tour.title: Demo Mode Is Contained on Purpose
tour.description: Demo mode ships invented numbers inside a product that customers use on real data, so its containment is deliberate and tested. `mode.ts` is the switch: a single `sessionStorage` token, never localStorage, never a cookie, never a build flag or environment variable, where only the exact string `on` counts as consent and every failure path returns off. `loaders.ts` is the only module that names a fixture, and it wraps each one in a dynamic `import()` so fixture code cannot enter the bundle while the switch is off — a guard test fails the build on any static value import from `fixtures/`. `useDemoQuery` uses TanStack Query's `enabled` so the loader never even runs in the off state, and demo screens like `PaymentsOverview` render `NotFound` rather than an empty shell, because a page that exists but says nothing invites "is it broken?".
tour.languageLesson: `DemoContext` uses a lazy `useState` initialiser so `?demo=1` is resolved exactly once per mount. Re-running it on every location change would let a later link carrying `?demo=0` silently flip the switch mid-session.

tour.title: src/docs Is a Feature, Not Documentation
tour.description: The name misleads everyone once: `src/docs/` is not documentation about this codebase, it is the in-app user-guide viewer and command palette. Its corpus does not exist on disk — `scripts/build-docs-index.mjs` walks `docs/user-guide` at build time, splits pages into sections, syntax-highlights fenced code with Shiki in Node, resolves cross-links, and emits `src/generated/docs.json`. `useDocs.ts` loads that bundled payload as a dynamic import and caches the promise at module scope so the palette and the panel share one fetch, and `search.ts` scores roughly 501 short sections per keystroke with no search library and no prebuilt index. The whole feature works offline.
tour.languageLesson: The generator only writes its output when invoked directly, comparing `import.meta.url` against `argv[1]`. That is the ESM equivalent of Python's `if __name__ == "__main__"`, and it is what lets tests import `buildCorpus` without the import itself writing a file.

tour.title: Build, Modes and the Product Guard
tour.description: The tour closes where Step 1 opened. One `vite.config.ts` serves both products — Vite is invoked with a per-product root and `--mode` — and it carries the `/dashboard/` base path, the `@` alias, the Vitest jsdom setup and a dev proxy forwarding `/api`, `/manage`, `/platform` and `/ws` to the manage service on port 8081 (the comments record why 8081 and not the guard API's 8080). `verify-product-build.mjs` runs after the build and asserts the boundary actually held: the shared dashboard is present, the expected product title is baked in, and Codewall's endpoint surface appears in the Codewall bundle and only there. `apps/codewall/api/endpoints.ts` is the thing that guard is watching — product-specific API code kept up in `apps/`, deliberately out of shared `src/api/`.
tour.languageLesson: `verify-product-build.mjs` is a top-level-await ESM script that simply throws on failure, so the npm script's non-zero exit is the entire reporting mechanism. No test framework, no assertion library — the build either passes the boundary check or stops.
